books.section: Topic 1.4 Columbian Exchange, Spanish Exploration, and Conquest
The Conquistadores and the Defeat of Native Peoples
The Early Colonial Era: Spain Colonizes the New World

options.text: Epidemic disease devastated Native peoples while Native allies gave Spain vital military support.
The Mexica and Inca had no organized armies or tribute systems of their own.
options.misconception: Both were large, organized tribute empires with substantial armies.

options.text: Portugal supplied most of the soldiers, funding, and supplies for both expeditions.
options.misconception: Portugal supplied neither the soldiers nor the funding for these conquests.

options.text: Only Spanish caravels had the naval technology to carry armies across the Atlantic.
options.misconception: Portuguese and other vessels also crossed the Atlantic; ships alone explain nothing.

rationales.general:
1. Count the soldiers. Cortes landed with about 500 men against an empire's armies.
2. Ask what evened the odds. Epidemics were already killing far more people than any battle.
3. Add the allies. Thousands of Tlaxcalans joined Cortes against the Mexica, and Pizarro used divisions inside the Inca Empire.
4. Rule out the rest. Other ships crossed the ocean; both empires had armies; Portugal funded neither expedition.
Remember: when a small force wins fast, ask what was already weakening the other side.
rationales.A: Disease and Native allies were the decisive factors alongside Spanish arms. That is why small forces won so fast.
rationales.B: Both were large, organized tribute empires with substantial armies. The claim about them is false.
rationales.C: Portugal supplied neither the soldiers nor the funding for these conquests. Spain paid for its own expeditions.
rationales.D: Portuguese and other vessels also crossed the Atlantic. Ships alone explain nothing about the conquests.

stem: Small Spanish forces toppled the Mexica Empire (1519-1521) and seized the Inca ruler (1532) with astonishing speed. Which broader context is most important for explaining these rapid conquests?

stimulus.source_note: Paraphrase of Hernando Cortes, Second Letter to Charles V (October 30, 1520), public domain; quoted in 5 Steps to a 5 2024 Chapter 6.
stimulus.text: Paraphrase of Hernando Cortes, Second Letter to Charles V, October 30, 1520. Cortes describes throwing down the Mexica idols from the great temple in Tenochtitlan and putting images of the Virgin Mary and the saints in their place. The Mexica ruler Montezuma and the city's people warned him that if his actions became known throughout the country, the people would rise against him, because they believed their idols gave them all good things.
